newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank won't let rates fall too low.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank won't let rates fall too low.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank chief pledged to maintain an "appropriately loose" monetary policy but not let rates fall too low, saying easy money had not shown itself to be a "cure-all" for the island's sluggish economy.
"Currently consumer prices are stable, enabling the central bank to maintain a loose monetary policy to help economic development," governor Sheu Yuan-dong told reporters.

"But now liquidity has become slightly too loose. People and businesses can easily obtain enough money. The central bank will definitely try to maintain an appropriately loose policy, but not let interest rates too low so as not to hurt the interests of most depositors."

Sheu noted that five consecutive decreases in commercial banks' reserve requirements since mid-1995 had made money more accessible but had failed to reignite private investment in the island's sluggish economy.
"This shows that monetary policy is no cure-all medicine," Sheu said.
Further liberalisation was needed to bring unregulated or illegal finacing operations into legal channels.
"The finance ministry must open up the establishment of financing companies to legalise the current underground financing," Sheu said.

Sheu indicated he was unconcerned about outflows of Taiwan capital to rival China despite President Lee Teng-hui's regular statements that the island risked becoming too dependent on its main adversary's economy through excessive investment.
"According to our balance of payments report, Taiwan has shown capital outflows to China in the capital account, but in the current account, Taiwan has a big surplus," he said.
"Overall, Taiwan still has a net capital inflow from China. Capital outflow from Taiwan is not serious at all," he said.
"We should concern ourselves more with how to improve the domestic investment environment," She said.
